cards.front: What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?
cards.back: **Vertical** (scale up/down) = a bigger or smaller instance, e.g. `t3.micro` to `m7i.2xlarge`; capped by the largest size. **Horizontal** (scale out/in, elasticity) = more or fewer instances behind a load balancer; needs a distributed, ideally stateless app.

cards.front: What does high availability mean for an EC2 application?
cards.back: Running the same application in **at least two Availability Zones** (multi-AZ Auto Scaling group + multi-AZ load balancer) so the loss of one data center does not take it down.

cards.front: Name four benefits of putting a load balancer in front of EC2 instances.
cards.back: Any four of: one DNS entry point, spreads load, removes unhealthy instances via health checks, terminates TLS (HTTPS), cookie stickiness, spans AZs, separates public traffic from private traffic.

cards.front: What are the default ALB health check thresholds and interval?
cards.back: Interval **30 s**, timeout **5 s**, **5** consecutive successes to become healthy, **2** consecutive failures to become unhealthy, success code **200** (configurable within 200–499).

cards.front: Which load balancer works at layer 7 and routes by URL path, hostname, header, method, query string or source IP?
cards.back: The **Application Load Balancer** (ALB).

cards.front: What target types can an ALB target group use?
cards.back: **Instances** (often via an Auto Scaling group), **private IP addresses** (including on-premises over VPN/Direct Connect), and a **Lambda function** (request becomes a JSON event). ECS tasks register as instance or IP targets.

cards.front: Behind an ALB, how does the application find the client's real IP address?
cards.back: From the **X-Forwarded-For** header. **X-Forwarded-Proto** gives the client's protocol and **X-Forwarded-Port** the port. The TCP source the app sees is the ALB's private IP.

cards.front: Which load balancer gives you one static IP per AZ and lets you attach Elastic IPs?
cards.back: The **Network Load Balancer** (NLB). Useful when clients must allow-list fixed IP addresses.

cards.front: What protocols and target types does a Network Load Balancer support?
cards.back: Listeners: **TCP, UDP, TCP_UDP, TLS**, plus newer **QUIC/TCP_QUIC**. Targets: EC2 **instances**, private **IPs**, or an **ALB**. Health checks: TCP, HTTP or HTTPS.
cards.updated: QUIC and TCP_QUIC listeners are newer than the slides.

cards.front: You need static IPs for allow-listing AND HTTP path-based routing. What do you build?
cards.back: An **NLB with the ALB registered as its target** (NLB supplies static/Elastic IPs, ALB does layer 7 routing). **Global Accelerator** in front of the ALB is the other common answer.

cards.front: What is the Gateway Load Balancer for, and which protocol and port does it use?
cards.back: Deploying and scaling fleets of third-party **virtual appliances** (firewalls, IDS/IPS, deep packet inspection) as a transparent layer 3 gateway. It uses **GENEVE on port 6081**.

cards.front: How does traffic get sent to a Gateway Load Balancer?
cards.back: Through **Gateway Load Balancer endpoints** (a VPC endpoint type) that you set as the next hop in **route tables**.

cards.front: What is the recommended security group setup for EC2 instances behind a load balancer?
cards.back: Load balancer SG allows 80/443 from `0.0.0.0/0`; the instance SG allows the app port (and health check port) with the **load balancer's security group as the source**, so nobody can bypass the load balancer.

cards.front: Can a Network Load Balancer have security groups?
cards.back: Yes, but only if you attach at least one when you **create** it; an NLB created without security groups cannot get them later. (Gateway Load Balancers do not use security groups.)
cards.updated: NLB security group support was added after the original NLB design.

cards.front: What do sticky sessions do, and what is their main downside?
cards.back: They send the same client to the same target (session affinity) so locally stored session data is not lost. Downside: **uneven load** across targets, and the session is still lost if that target fails.

cards.front: Name the stickiness cookies: ALB duration-based, ALB application-based, ALB target-group-level, and CLB.
cards.back: ALB duration-based: **AWSALB**. ALB application-based: your own app cookie plus **AWSALBAPP**. Weighted target group stickiness: **AWSALBTG**. CLB: **AWSELB**. Don't use the AWSALB names for your own cookies.

cards.front: How does an NLB implement stickiness?
cards.back: By **source IP** affinity. It is not supported on TLS or QUIC listeners, and all clients behind one NAT share a source IP, so they land on the same target.

cards.front: What does cross-zone load balancing do?
cards.back: Each load balancer node spreads its traffic over **all registered targets in all enabled AZs**, not only those in its own AZ. Example: 1 target in AZ a, 4 in AZ b: on = 20% each; off = 50% for the AZ a target and 12.5% for each AZ b target.

cards.front: Cross-zone load balancing defaults and charges for ALB, NLB/GWLB and CLB?
cards.back: **ALB**: always on at LB level (can be turned off per target group), no inter-AZ charge. **NLB/GWLB**: off by default, inter-AZ data billed when on. **CLB**: on via console, off via API/CLI, no inter-AZ charge.
cards.updated: AWS docs say the CLB console pre-selects cross-zone; the slides say it is off by default.

cards.front: What is SNI and which load balancers support it?
cards.back: **Server Name Indication**: the client names the hostname in the TLS handshake so the server can present the matching certificate from several. Supported by **ALB, NLB and CloudFront**, not the CLB.

cards.front: How do you serve several HTTPS domains with different certificates on a Classic Load Balancer?
cards.back: You can't use SNI on a CLB: each HTTPS listener has **one certificate**. Use one CLB per certificate, a single certificate covering all names (SAN or wildcard), or migrate to an ALB.

cards.front: What does an HTTPS listener need, and where do the certificates come from?
cards.back: Exactly one **default certificate**, an optional **certificate list** (up to 25 by default) and a **security policy** for TLS versions/ciphers. Certificates come from **ACM** (free, auto-renewed public certs) or are imported/uploaded to ACM or IAM.

cards.front: How long are ACM public certificates valid today?
cards.back: **198 days** (since 18 February 2026, previously 395), to meet the CA/Browser Forum 200-day limit. ACM renews them automatically.
cards.updated: Validity changed from 395 to 198 days in February 2026.

cards.front: What is deregistration delay (connection draining) and its range and default?
cards.back: Time for in-flight requests to finish while a target is deregistering; no new requests go to it. ALB/NLB/GWLB **deregistration delay**: 0–3600 s (0 disables). CLB **connection draining**: 1–3600 s. Default **300 s** for both.

cards.front: When would you lower the deregistration delay, and when would you raise it?
cards.back: **Lower** it (e.g. 10–30 s) when requests are short, so deployments and scale-in finish faster. **Raise** it for long-running requests such as large uploads or downloads, so they are not cut off.

cards.front: What happens when every target in an ALB or NLB target group fails its health checks?
cards.back: The load balancer **fails open**: it sends traffic to all targets regardless of health, rather than returning nothing.

cards.front: Internet-facing vs internal load balancer: what is the difference?
cards.back: **Internet-facing** nodes have public IPs and serve internet clients. **Internal** nodes have only private IPs and serve clients inside the VPC or connected networks. Both reach targets using **private IPs**, so targets need no public IPs.

cards.front: What is the status of the Classic Load Balancer today?
cards.back: AWS calls it the **previous generation** and recommends migrating to an ALB or NLB. It supports HTTP, HTTPS, TCP and SSL, has no target groups or content-based routing, and no SNI.
cards.updated: AWS docs now label the CLB as previous generation with a migration recommendation.
